name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,211

clue.text: Makeshift quantity of butter he’d put in cup

indicators.note: to put something in a vessel is to place it inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: a pat is a small flat portion of butter
taken as written
the contraction with its apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A cook improvises by dropping a knob of butter into a cup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quantity of butter' sounds like a recipe measure, but a pat is the small slab served at table; the contraction he'd loses its apostrophe before going in.
explanation.definitionFit: Something hastily repaired with whatever was at hand is temporary and improvised, the sense of a stopgap fix.

clue.text: Servant opening up over closure of palace

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, backwards
the closure of a word is its end, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: a gap is an opening
the final letter of palace

explanation.surface: A palace servant opens up as the building closes for the night.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' means placed above, so the reversed piece sits on top of the palace's final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A page was historically a boy employed as an attendant to a noble household, so a kind of servant.

clue.text: Compliment family welcoming aunt regularly

indicators.note: doing something regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept
welcoming someone takes them inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a tribe is an extended family group
second and fourth letters of aunt

explanation.surface: A family pays a compliment by warmly receiving their aunt.
explanation.walkthrough: The even letters of aunt are U and T, which slot into TRIBE before its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A tribute is an act or statement of praise and respect, so a compliment paid to someone.

clue.text: Attractive MC disowning son

indicators.note: to disown is to cast off, so a letter is thrown out

blocks.note: a master of ceremonies hosts a show
S is the standard abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A good-looking master of ceremonies cuts off his son.
explanation.walkthrough: MC is short for master of ceremonies, the host of an event; take S out of HOST.
explanation.definitionFit: In informal speech hot describes someone sexually appealing or good-looking.

clue.text: Doctor to act badly around university city

indicators.note: to be around something is to encircle it, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: DR is the abbreviation for doctor
U is the abbreviation for university
to ham is to overact

explanation.surface: A doctor behaves poorly in a famous university town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'university city' reads as one phrase, but university belongs to the wordplay. Durham is a cathedral city in northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Durham is an English cathedral settlement in the north-east, home to one of Britain's oldest universities.

clue.text: Little change about English idiot? A sorry state

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the coins wrap around what follows

blocks.note: pennies are small change in Britain
a nit is a fool
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a little spare change for a foolish Englishman leaves him in a sorry state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little change' means small coins, the British pennies; the insertion goes after the second letter. Nit is a mild British word for an idiot.
explanation.definitionFit: Penitence is the condition of feeling remorse for wrongdoing, being sorry in a moral sense.

clue.text: Pet fur? Nothing shed

indicators.note: shed means cast off, so a letter drops away

blocks.note: an animal's fur is its coat
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Someone asks about pet hair, and the answer is that none has been shed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pet fur' reads as one phrase, but Pet is the definition and fur the wordplay; remove O from COAT.
explanation.definitionFit: The domestic feline is one of the most common animals kept as a companion at home.

clue.text: Conservative General Assembly dance

blocks.note: CON is the abbreviation for Conservative
the initials of General Assembly, as the UN body is often written

explanation.surface: Tories at a General Assembly break into a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: Both abbreviations are standard: CON for a Conservative party member, GA for a General Assembly.
explanation.definitionFit: The conga is a Latin American line dance in which people follow one another in single file.

clue.text: In the morning, diving into the southern river

indicators.note: something diving into water ends up inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: taken as written
AM, ante meridiem, means before noon
S is the abbreviation for southern

explanation.surface: Someone takes an early-morning plunge into a river in the south.
explanation.walkthrough: The definite article in the clue is wordplay, not grammar. The Thames flows through London in southern England.
explanation.definitionFit: The Thames is the major English waterway that runs through Oxford and London to the North Sea.

clue.text: Glamour in good collection of puppies?

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
a litter is the young born to a dog at one time

explanation.surface: Glamour shows up in a fine batch of puppies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a container signal, but it only links the definition to the charade.
explanation.definitionFit: Glitter is figurative sparkle, showy attractiveness or glamour, as in the glitter of show business.

clue.text: Some assassin in Japan

indicators.note: some of a phrase is only part of it, so the letters lie within the words that follow

blocks.note: the run straddles the last letter of the first word, the middle word, and the start of the last

explanation.surface: A description of a kind of killer from Japanese history.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and the hiding place: the letters run across assassiN IN JApan.
explanation.definitionFit: Ninjas were covert agents of feudal Japan trained in espionage, sabotage and killing.

clue.text: Confirm nastiest tuba is melted down

indicators.note: metal melted down is recast into a new shape, so the letters are reformed

blocks.note: the letters of both words

explanation.surface: Someone confirms that the worst brass instrument has been sent for scrap.
explanation.walkthrough: All twelve letters of the two middle words rearrange to form the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To substantiate a claim is to provide evidence proving it true, so to confirm or verify it.

clue.text: Time to support distribution of musical’s programme on different media?

indicators.note: distributing things spreads them out in a new arrangement
in a down entry, a supporting piece holds up the rest, so it goes at the bottom

blocks.note: the letters of the word, apostrophe ignored
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A show's time slot is arranged to support the release of a musical across platforms.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters of musical's sit on top, with T beneath them as support.
explanation.definitionFit: A simulcast is a broadcast transmitted at the same time on more than one channel, such as radio and television.

clue.text: Hard wood is what steerer holds

blocks.note: H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
elm is a kind of timber

explanation.surface: A sailor's wheel or tiller is made of tough timber.
explanation.walkthrough: H for hard comes from pencil grades.
explanation.definitionFit: The helm is a ship's wheel or tiller, the control a helmsman grips to guide the vessel.

clue.text: Boy returned hot food

indicators.note: returned means going back, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a son is a boy
H is the tap abbreviation for hot

explanation.surface: A lad came back with a hot meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hot food' reads as a single phrase, but hot gives H; nosh is informal British slang for food.
explanation.definitionFit: Nosh is a colloquial word for food or a meal, from Yiddish via British slang.

clue.text: Winter sport takings revived

indicators.note: something revived is brought back in fresh form, so the letters are remade

blocks.note: the letters of the word

explanation.surface: Box-office receipts for a winter sport have picked up again.
explanation.walkthrough: Takings means money taken in, but here it is only a set of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Gliding on ice with bladed boots is a classic cold-season pastime and Olympic event.

clue.text: Question one kidnapping a sailor from Arab country

indicators.note: a kidnapper holds a captive, so one piece is held within another

blocks.note: Q is the abbreviation for question
I is the Roman numeral one
taken as written
a tar is a sailor

explanation.surface: Someone asks about a person who snatched a sailor from a Gulf state.
explanation.walkthrough: Q and I together form QI, which holds A and TAR. 'from Arab country' wants to be wordplay, but it is the adjectival definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Qatari is the adjective describing people or things belonging to Qatar, a Gulf state on the Arabian peninsula.

clue.text: I am at end of line welcoming new resident

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, which alone is kept
welcoming a guest brings them inside, so one piece enters another

blocks.note: I'm contracts I am
taken as written
the last letter of line
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Someone waiting at the back of a queue greets a newcomer to the building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I am' is contracted to I'm; the new letter slips in just after the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An inmate is a person living in an institution such as a prison or hospital, an occupant there.

clue.text: Emergency worker can name album that’s playing

indicators.note: playing with something moves it about, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters of all three words

explanation.surface: A paramedic is able to identify whichever record is on.
explanation.walkthrough: The three middle words supply exactly twelve letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: An ambulanceman is a crew member who drives or staffs a vehicle carrying the sick and injured to hospital.

clue.text: Dull person endlessly referring to chemical element

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is removed

blocks.note: a bore is a tedious person
on means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A tedious speaker drones on forever about a chemistry topic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'referring to' means about, which crosswords often render as a two-letter preposition.
explanation.definitionFit: Boron is element number five on the periodic table, a metalloid used in glass and detergents.

clue.text: Celebrity’s backing singers

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the letters run in the other direction

blocks.note: rats are informers, who sing to the police

explanation.surface: A celebrity's backing singers, as in a pop concert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing singers' looks like a musical phrase, but backing is the signal; singers are informers in criminal slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A star is a famous performer or public figure, a well-known name in entertainment.

clue.text: Skill retaining O and A in key supply of blood

indicators.note: to retain is to keep hold of, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: art is skill
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A skill to keep O and A in a key, like a musical scale.
explanation.walkthrough: ART holds O after its first letter, and 'and' adds A at the end. 'key' wants to be a musical note; it belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The aorta is the body's main artery, carrying oxygenated blood from the heart to the rest of the body.

clue.text: Emergency mission, perhaps, first couple of chaps having fallen from mountain transport

indicators.note: the first couple of a word are its opening two letters
something that has fallen from a place is no longer there, so it is removed

blocks.note: the opening two letters of chaps, as first couple asks
a chairlift carries skiers up a mountain

explanation.surface: On a rescue operation, a couple of men tumble off a ski lift.
explanation.walkthrough: Take CH from the front of CHAIRLIFT; 'perhaps' marks the definition as one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An airlift transports people or supplies by aircraft, often as urgent relief, so a rescue flight is one instance.

clue.text: Sprint disaster — I must drop out

indicators.note: dropping out means leaving, so a letter goes missing

blocks.note: ruin is a disaster
taken as written

explanation.surface: A racer laments a disastrous dash that forces them to withdraw.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove I from RUIN.
explanation.definitionFit: To sprint is to move at speed on foot, and as nouns a sprint is a short fast dash.

clue.text: Popular name for place to get drinks

blocks.note: in means fashionable or popular
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A well-liked name for a bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Popular name' reads as one phrase, but each word gives its own piece.
explanation.definitionFit: An inn is a pub or small hotel where travellers can buy alcohol and meals.

clue.text: Precocious child — great new source of exasperation, possibly

indicators.note: a source is where something starts, so only the first letter is kept
possibly signals one of several possible arrangements of the letters

blocks.note: the letters of both words
the first letter of exasperation

explanation.surface: A cheeky youngster is a great fresh cause of irritation.
explanation.walkthrough: The eight letters of the two words plus E from exasperation are rearranged together.
explanation.definitionFit: A tweenager is a child between about ten and twelve who behaves older than their years, hence forward or precocious.
